content:
Earlier this year I swapped a petrol-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the lawn boundary to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot automatically mows according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think many people may find this machine easier to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to first drive the mower with my phone along the boundary before it could build an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. The mower is equipped with three cameras that can automatically map out the lawn area, requiring neither buried boundary wires nor an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less familiar with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mother, who lives in another U.S. state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 entirely on her own, without any assistance from me. She said everything worked fine. That said, though, I'm not entirely sure she had the patience to first drive the robot with her phone along the entire boundary and then mark out all the areas to avoid.

During the automatic mapping in the front yard, a few minor issues cropped up. There's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was solved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when building the initial map.

A look through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used the iPhone's screen-mirroring feature to cast that video onto the big screen of my Mac. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the back garden.

This feature isn't necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and can sometimes explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 has no equivalent live camera view.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share many features. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zones, no-go markers, and remote control of the mower.

When it comes to that last feature, the TerraMow's design is particularly thoughtful. In addition to traditional left/right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, with no need for human intervention. That said, the TerraMow's joystick mode is quite handy for trimming small patches the robot may have missed.

Sometimes I almost felt like I was controlling the robot by telepathy (the fun kind of way). Holding the iPhone and walking behind the mower, a gentle nudge with my thumb and the robot would steer precisely to where I wanted it to go.

Every robotic mower app should copy this design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground and was noticeably louder in operation.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is "very loud", but the difference is clearly noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly — even when it goes out at night with its headlights on, you can almost forget it's still running.

Because the TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. As a result, scheduling mowing during the day becomes even more important.

The V1000 feels solidly built, and it's also larger than the Anthbot M9. The TerraMow package includes a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed consistently. I left it to mow every day for several weeks in a row and never needed any human intervention.

When adaptive mapping gets a little too "clever"

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower constantly adjusts its map based on what it sees and hears. Each time it finishes a job, saving those changes takes a fairly long time, during which you can't do anything in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting extreme case. Water had pooled in one part of the yard, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the skipped circular patch, the weeds grew taller and taller. After a while, the taller weeds in that spot seemed to fool the mower into thinking they were something to avoid permanently, and even after the ground dried out, the area kept being skipped.

I used the app's remote control to manually drive the mower over there and cut down the taller weeds, and the problem was solved. Once that area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as well.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Otherwise, taller grass growing along an indistinct boundary can be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. That method requires more preparation work, but it avoids the map "changing its mind" about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac conclusion

Having used both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending the TerraMow's camera-led approach.

For me, burying wires in the ground is simply not an option, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining additional hardware. The TerraMow needs neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, indistinct boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a patch of overgrown weeds for a permanent obstacle.

All of those issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, engaging live camera views, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I really enjoy tending the garden, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that chore over to a robot frees up time for looking after the flower beds, doing the edging, and taking care of detail work, while keeping the lawn neat.

The TerraMow V1000 excels at this, and I would recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but doesn't want to bury wires in the ground, doesn't want to install an RTK antenna, and doesn't want to walk the entire yard holding a phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently lists the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, and a US$200 coupon code is available on the deals site. The product can also be purchased through TerraMow's official website.
